chapter.name: Light: Mirrors and Lenses
chapter.blurb: Meena's visit to a science centre, where curved mirrors make her reflection look strangely large, small or upside down, opens this chapter on spherical mirrors and lenses: concave and convex mirrors and how the images they form change with the object's distance, the two laws of reflection linking the angle of incidence to the angle of reflection, how spherical mirrors converge or diverge parallel beams of light, and can even concentrate sunlight enough to burn paper, and convex and concave lenses, which behave in much the same way but let light pass through rather than reflecting it, with everyday uses from eyeglasses and cameras to telescopes, microscopes and the lens inside our own eye.

scope_in.item: Introduction: Meena's visit to a science centre and unusual curved mirrors
10.1 What Are Spherical Mirrors: spherical, concave and convex mirrors; the spoon activity; how spherical mirrors are actually made and which surface is coated
Activity 10.2: distinguishing concave and convex mirrors by viewing them from the side

10.2 What Are the Characteristics of Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors: image size and orientation in concave, convex and plane mirrors as object distance changes; lateral inversion; everyday uses of concave and convex mirrors (torches, headlights, dental mirrors, telescopes, side-view mirrors, road safety and store surveillance mirrors)

10.3 What Are the Laws of Reflection: incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, the two laws of reflection and their validity for all mirrors; Our scientific heritage box on Bhaskara II-era astronomers using bowls of water

Activity 10.6 and 10.7: parallel beams converging (concave) or diverging (convex) on reflection, and concentrating sunlight with a concave mirror to produce heat; solar concentrators, solar cookers and solar furnaces

10.4 What Is a Lens: a lens as a transparent, curved material; the water-drop lens activity; the magnifying glass; convex and concave lens shapes; how the image seen through a convex or concave lens changes with the object's distance

Activity 10.10 and 10.11: parallel beams passing through a flat glass plate, converging through a convex lens, diverging through a concave lens; concentrating sunlight with a convex lens; everyday uses of lenses (eyeglasses, cameras, telescopes, microscopes, the eye's own lens); chapter summary (Snapshots)

concepts.name: Spherical mirrors: concave and convex
concepts.description: Spherical mirrors are curved mirrors shaped like part of a hollow glass sphere; a concave mirror's reflecting surface curves inwards and a convex mirror's curves outwards.
concepts.idea: A mirror whose reflecting surface is curved like part of a hollow sphere is a spherical mirror, and it is called concave or convex depending on which way that surface curves.
concepts.rule: Curved mirrors, like the two sides of a shiny metallic spoon, can also be specially made. Spherical mirrors are a common type of curved mirror shaped like a part of a hollow glass sphere; mirrors whose reflecting surfaces are spherical are called spherical mirrors. A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inwards is called a concave mirror. A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves outwards is called a convex mirror. In diagrams, the non-reflecting surface of a mirror is shown shaded. Spherical mirrors are not literally cut from a hollow glass sphere; instead they are created by grinding and polishing a flat piece of glass into a curved surface. If a reflective coating, such as a thin layer of aluminium, is applied on the outer curved surface, it forms a concave mirror, because light reflects off the untouched inner curved surface. If the coating is applied on the inner curved surface, it forms a convex mirror, because light reflects off the outer curved surface. To tell a concave mirror from a convex mirror lying flat on a table, view it from the side, at the level of its reflecting surface, to see whether that surface curves inwards or outwards.
concepts.example: Looking into the inner, curved-inward surface of a shiny spoon shows an inverted image, like a concave mirror; looking into its outer, bulging surface shows an erect but smaller image, like a convex mirror.

concepts.name: Characteristics of images formed by spherical mirrors, and their uses
concepts.description: How the size and orientation of an image formed by a concave or convex mirror changes with the object's distance, and where each type of mirror is used in daily life.
concepts.idea: A concave mirror's image changes from erect and enlarged, close up, to inverted and shrinking, farther away; a convex mirror's image is always erect and diminished, and each behaviour is put to use in different everyday devices.
concepts.rule: In a concave mirror, when the object is placed close to the mirror, the image is erect but larger than the object, that is, enlarged. When the object is moved farther away, the image becomes inverted; it is initially enlarged and then keeps getting smaller. In a convex mirror, the image is always erect and smaller than the object, that is, diminished, though its size decreases slightly as the object moves away. A plane mirror, unlike these, always forms an erect image of the same size as the object. Lateral inversion is seen in all three types of mirrors. Concave mirrors are used as reflectors in torches and vehicle headlights, and as dental mirrors, which give an enlarged view of teeth when held close; the main mirror of a reflecting telescope is also a large concave mirror. Convex mirrors are used as side-view mirrors on vehicles, since they always give an erect image of the traffic behind, smaller than the actual vehicles, and cover a much wider area of the road; they are also installed at road intersections and sharp bends so drivers from both sides can see each other, and in big stores to monitor a large area and deter theft.
concepts.example: A dentist's concave mirror held close to a tooth gives an enlarged, erect view of it, while a vehicle's convex side-view mirror gives a wide but diminished, erect view of the traffic behind.

concepts.name: Laws of reflection
concepts.description: The incident ray, normal and reflected ray, the angle of incidence and angle of reflection, and the two laws of reflection that hold for every mirror.
concepts.idea: Light reflecting off any mirror obeys two laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
concepts.rule: We represent light by straight lines with arrows, called rays, showing the path light travels. The ray of light that falls on a mirror is called the incident ray, and the ray that comes back from the mirror is called the reflected ray. The normal is a line drawn perpendicular, at 90 degrees, to the mirror at the point of incidence. The angle between the normal and the incident ray is the angle of incidence (i); the angle between the normal and the reflected ray is the angle of reflection (r). Careful measurement shows the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection; this is the first law of reflection. If the incident ray falls along the normal, both angles are zero. The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane; this is the second law of reflection, shown by the fact that bending the paper on which the beam is drawn makes the reflected beam disappear from the bent, differently angled part. These laws of reflection are valid for all kinds of mirrors, plane, concave and convex alike. More than 800 years ago, around the time of the Indian mathematician Bhaskara II, astronomers used shallow bowls of water to observe stars and planets, measuring their positions from the reflected images seen through tubes placed at angles, suggesting a practical understanding of reflection even though the laws were not written down.
concepts.example: A ray of light striking a mirror at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees reflects at an angle of reflection of 30 degrees, since the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection.

concepts.name: Spherical mirrors, parallel beams, and concentrating light
concepts.description: How a concave mirror converges and a convex mirror diverges a set of parallel light rays, and how a concave mirror concentrates sunlight enough to produce heat.
concepts.idea: A concave mirror brings parallel rays of light together at a point, concentrating their energy, while a convex mirror spreads parallel rays apart.
concepts.rule: When multiple parallel beams of light fall upon a plane mirror, the reflected beams stay parallel. When multiple parallel beams fall upon a concave mirror, the reflected beams get closer together, that is, they converge. When they fall upon a convex mirror, the reflected beams spread out, that is, they diverge. Even though each ray of light still obeys the laws of reflection at the point it strikes the curved surface, the curved shape of a spherical mirror causes the overall parallel beam to converge or diverge, depending on whether the mirror is concave or convex. Since a concave mirror converges light, holding one with its reflecting surface facing the Sun and directing the reflected sunlight onto a sheet of paper produces a small, sharp, bright spot where the Sun's light is concentrated; holding this steady can make the paper smoke or catch fire, because the concentrated light produces enough heat there. This activity must always be done under the supervision of a teacher or adult, never looking towards the Sun or into the mirror reflecting it, and focusing the light only on paper, never towards a person's face or eyes. Devices that concentrate sunlight into a small area using mirrors and lenses are called solar concentrators; the concentrated sunlight can be used to heat a liquid to produce steam for generating electricity, for large-scale cooking, or in solar furnaces, which are even used to melt steel.
concepts.example: Holding a concave mirror facing the Sun and adjusting the distance of a sheet of paper until a sharp, bright spot forms shows the mirror converging the Sun's parallel rays to one concentrated point.

concepts.name: Lenses: convex and concave, and how they form images
concepts.description: A lens is a piece of transparent, curved material, convex or concave, and light passes through it rather than reflecting; the image seen through a convex or concave lens depends on its shape and the object's distance.
concepts.idea: A convex lens, thicker in the middle, forms an erect enlarged image close up and an inverted, shrinking image farther away, while a concave lens, thicker at the edges, always forms an erect, diminished image.
concepts.rule: A lens is a piece of transparent material, usually glass or plastic, which has curved surfaces. Unlike mirrors, lenses allow light to pass through them, so we see things through a lens rather than in a lens. A curved drop of water placed over text, with its surface curved outward, acts like a simple lens: the letters beneath it appear larger, the same way a magnifying glass makes small print appear bigger. A lens which is thicker at the middle than at the edges is called a convex lens; a lens which is thicker at the edges than at the middle is called a concave lens. When an object is placed close to a convex lens and viewed through it, the image appears erect and enlarged; as the object moves farther away, the image becomes inverted, first enlarged in size and then diminishing. An object viewed through a concave lens always appears erect and diminished, though its size changes somewhat as its distance from the lens changes.
concepts.example: Looking through a curved drop of water placed over printed text makes the letters underneath appear larger, the same way a magnifying glass, a convex lens, enlarges small print.

concepts.name: Lenses, parallel beams, and everyday uses
concepts.description: A convex lens converges and a concave lens diverges a beam of parallel light rays, while a flat glass plate does neither, and lenses are used all around us, including inside our own eye.
concepts.idea: A convex lens is a converging lens that can even concentrate sunlight enough to burn paper, a concave lens is a diverging lens, and this converging or diverging behaviour is what makes lenses useful in eyeglasses, cameras, telescopes, microscopes and our own eye.
concepts.rule: When multiple parallel beams of light are passed through a thin transparent glass plate, they pass through as they are. When passed through a convex lens, the beams converge, come together, which is why a convex lens is also called a converging lens. When passed through a concave lens, the beams diverge, spread apart, which is why a concave lens is also called a diverging lens. Because it converges light, a convex lens, like a concave mirror, can be used to focus sunlight into a small area and burn paper, and the same safety rule applies: never look at the Sun directly or through the lens. Lenses are used everywhere around us: the eyeglasses people wear to see clearly are lenses, and cameras, telescopes and microscopes all use lenses to work. Even our own eye has a convex lens inside it, an amazing lens that can change its own shape, which is what allows us to read a book held close or see something far away.
concepts.example: A convex lens focusing sunlight to a small bright spot that can make paper smoke is the same converging behaviour that a camera lens uses to focus light from a scene into a sharp photograph.
